source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: Hits come from mostly conventional work with a small atypical tail. Conventionality alone or novelty alone gives much less.
numbers: 17.9M Web of Science papers. Hit = top 5% of citations at 8 years. Hit rate per 100 papers: high conventionality plus tail novelty 9.11; conventional only 5.82; novel only 5.33; neither 2.05. Peak impact at the 85th-95th percentile of median conventionality.
limits: Journal-pair z-scores only. Citations as outcome. Correlational. Hit rate about 2x background, not a causal effect.
agent_relevance: Rule for open mode: keep most of an attempt standard and add one or two far links.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Atypical combinations, prevalence results
finding: Most papers are highly conventional. Atypical journal pairs are rare, and this holds field by field.
numbers: Half of papers have median z above 69.0 (1980s) and 99.5 (1990s). Median z below 0 in only 3.54% (1980s) and 2.67% (1990s). 10th-percentile z below 0 in 40.8% (1980s) and 40.7% (1990s). 40.1% of interdisciplinary journal pairs were novel.
limits: Journal level, not idea level.
agent_relevance: Free sampling drifts to the conventional centre. Tail moves may need to be forced.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Atypical combinations, team results
finding: Teams add tail novelty without losing conventionality. Larger teams get more impact at nearly every mix. The peak holds with and without tail novelty.
numbers: Regression per each of 11 conventionality bins and team size, field fixed effects. Tail novelty differs by team size (K-S P<0.001); median conventionality does not.
limits: Team size is confounded with citation reach. Later work (b08, b13, b24) disputes team-size effects on disruption.
agent_relevance: Several independent attempts combined may reach the mixed profile more often than one attempt.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas?
finding: Atypicality and disruption capture different processes. Atypicality is cross-topic extension of known ideas. Disruption is replacement of a dominant idea inside its own topic. They correlate negatively.
numbers: About 41M articles 1965-2020 (OpenAlex). Top 5% atypical A>22.9; top 5% disruptive D>0.04. Negative A-D link across disciplines, periods and team sizes. LLM (Llama-3.1-70B) topical similarity to top reference: high for disruptive papers, low for atypical papers. 50,147 disruptive papers classified theory vs method; theories are displaced more slowly.
quote: A novel combination (like a hypothetical microwave TV) may be creative, but it is unlikely to replace either
limits: The correlation coefficient is not stated in the text. The LLM classifier is zero-shot; only prompt-robustness checked. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Two operators need two selection rules: recombine from distant areas, or replace the dominant answer to the same question. Do not score both with one novelty number.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Earlier paper by overlapping authors. Highly atypical papers are more often disruptive than conventional ones, yet the paper-level correlation is slightly negative.
numbers: Highly novel papers disrupt in 61% vs 36% of conventional ones (nearly 2x). Pearson r between typicality and D = -0.05 (p<0.001). 2.3% of papers highly atypical; share fell from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000). 67% of papers have D<0. D needs about 10 years to reach 80% of its final value. Journal-embedding inner product vs z-score r=0.74.
limits: Tension with b04, which reports a negative A-D link at full scale. Answers depend on the cut (extreme bins vs whole sample). The effect is stronger in artificial than natural sciences.
agent_relevance: Report novelty effects across the tail, not as one average.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies
finding: Risky strategies pay more on average, not enough to offset failure risk. Prize winners gamble more.
numbers: Biomedical chemistry network. Repeat 85.8% vs new/jump 14.2% of statements; new bridges 12.4% vs jumps 1.8%. Mean citations 8.38 repeat, 11.00 new, 12.90 jump (1983-2002). Break-even needs new and jump to succeed 76% and 65% as often as repeat. Surprisal explains 29.2% of variation in mean citations. 137 prizes analysed.
limits: Citations as reward. One field. Means, not tails.
agent_relevance: Far moves have higher expected reward but high variance. An agent with several attempts can afford the variance more cheaply than one human.

source: Chen, Bornmann, Bu (2025) Dynamic disruption index across citation and cited-references windows
finding: Disruption scores need long windows to be stable.
numbers: A 10-year window gives over 80% agreement with final D class. 3-year windows are unstable. Papers with 30 or more references stabilise 1-3 years faster. Top and bottom 5% D are identifiable within 5 years. Four fields.
limits: Cutoffs depend on field.
agent_relevance: Disruption is a late signal. It cannot serve as a live selection score.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) Team size and its negative impact on the disruption index
finding: The small-team advantage survives their robustness checks but flips sign with a 5-year window.
numbers: Original Wu et al. 2019 used 65M papers, patents, software 1954-2014. Negative link holds after controls for reference length, citations, time. A 5-year window shows a positive link.
limits: Written by the original authors. Contested by b13, b24.
agent_relevance: Metric windows can reverse conclusions. Test a rule at the horizon it will be judged on.

source: Liang, Jiang, Hou (2020) Same data may bring conflict results: a caution to use the disruptive index
finding: Disruption depends on citation window, discipline and year. Not every paper with D=1 is a breakthrough.
numbers: Nobel prize-winning articles 1900-2016 vs benchmark articles, median D per year, Medicine vs Chemistry vs Physics. Different windows give different, even opposite, results.
limits: Small set. No single effect size.
agent_relevance: Disruption cannot be a gold label for the agent's choice rule.

source: Bornmann, Devarakonda, Tekles, Chacko (2020) Are disruption index indicators convergently valid?
finding: Disruption variants did not track expert 'new finding' tags. The original index loaded negatively on a citation-impact factor.
numbers: 120,179 F1000Prime papers 2000-2016. 45 Poisson regressions. For 'New finding' the percentage-change coefficients were negative (-2.71, -0.62, -2.13, -2.13). 'Technical advance' was positive (6.72 to 20.65). 'Refutation' was negative (-9.28 to -14.83). One variant (5) agreed with expectations most often.
limits: F1000 reviewers lean toward well-cited papers. Weak external criterion.
agent_relevance: Disruption is not newness as experts see it. Keep two separate measures.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: Failed replication of the 'science is less disruptive' result. The decline in Park et al. 2023 comes from records with zero references and CD=1.
numbers: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents with CD5=1 were hidden by a plotting bug. 97% of CD5=1 papers and 78% of CD5=1 patents have zero recorded references. Of 100 sampled each, 93% of papers and 98% of patents do cite references in the PDF. A zero-reference dummy lifts R2 from 0.10 to 0.52 (patents) and 0.15 to 0.95 (papers). Random rewiring reproduces the decline.
quote: A bug in the seaborn 0.11.2 plotting software silently drops the largest data points
limits: Shows the headline test was invalid, not that disruption did not decline. Park et al. original not opened (PDF damaged this session).
agent_relevance: Check data before reading a trend. Records with no evidence can fake a signal. The same holds for our own scorers.

source: Petersen, Arroyave, Pammolli (2023) The disruption index is biased by citation inflation
finding: The decline in the disruption index tracks growing reference lists and self-citation, not innovation.
numbers: Total citations grow 5.1% a year (0.033 paper growth plus 0.018 reference growth), doubling every 13.6 years. Three lines: deduction, Microsoft Academic Graph data, synthetic networks.
limits: Mechanism is mathematical and model-based.
agent_relevance: Normalise scores for length. A longer plan or more cited sources lowers a diffusion-type score by construction.

source: Petersen, Arroyave, Pammolli (2024) The disruption index suffers from citation inflation and is confounded by shifts in citation practice
finding: Extended version: disruptiveness rose slightly 2005-2015 in SciSciNet, and the negative team-size relation is tiny.
numbers: Quasi-experiment: PNAS vs PNAS Plus, which differ in length. Team-size effect shifts from negative to positive at 8 or more coauthors.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; methods not read in depth.
agent_relevance: Same as b12.

source: Bentley, Valverde, Borycz, Vidiella, Horne, Duran-Nebreda, O'Brien (2023) Is disruption decreasing, or is it accelerating?
finding: A citation-weighted disruption index on the same data is near neutral for 50 years and modestly up since 2000.
numbers: Papers and citations both grow exponentially (about 4-5% a year). Unweighted CD5 counts a paper with 2 citations and CD=-1 as offsetting one with 1,000 citations and CD=+1.
limits: The weighted index is the authors' own and not independently validated.
agent_relevance: The choice of aggregate changes the answer.

source: Macher, Rutzer, Weder (2026) Is there a secular decline in disruptive patents? Correcting for measurement bias
finding: For patents, most of the reported decline comes from truncating backward citations before 1976.
numbers: 88% of the decrease in mean CD index over 1980-2010 is explained by the truncation. The number of highly disruptive patents has risen since 1980, especially since 2008.
limits: Patents only.
agent_relevance: Results from one corpus may not transfer to another.

source: Wu, Wu, Park, Leahey, Funk (2026) Is innovation becoming less disruptive? An inventory of the literature
finding: Inventory of 105 studies. Most report decline across papers, patents, products, law, music and art, in text-based and citation-based methods. Some rebounds and field-lifecycle variation exist.
numbers: 105 studies catalogued.
limits: Authors include Funk and Park, whose index is under dispute (b11-b15). Novelty literature excluded by design.
agent_relevance: Rising atypical share with falling disruption is the pattern b04 explains. A population claim, not an agent rule.

source: Fang and Evans (2025) Generalization and the rise of system-level creativity in science
finding: Splitting contributions into foundation, extension and generalization shows innovation moved between fields. The disruption index mixes modes.
numbers: Foundation and extension works fell after the 1990s; generalization rose. Top generalizing works reach 84.0% farther in reference space, 15.5% farther in semantic space, and are 114.0% more likely to receive cross-domain citations. In one subset the disruption index fell 57.6% (0.059 in 1950 to 0.025 in 1990) while the extension index rose from 0.536 to 0.762.
limits: Their own new indices, not externally validated. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A third operator: build an answer others reuse across areas.

source: Yu and Romero (2024) Does the use of unusual combinations of datasets contribute to greater scientific impact?
finding: Unusual dataset pairs bring more citations. Topic atypicality adds much less.
numbers: More than 30,000 social science papers using over 5,000 ICPSR datasets. Data combination: about 15% more citations at 3, 5 and 10 years vs single dataset; controlling for topic atypicality leaves 1-4%. Smaller and less experienced teams use atypical data combinations more.
limits: One discipline. Citation outcome. Percentages read from messy text extraction.
agent_relevance: Vary the evidence used, not only the framing.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review judged LLM ideas as more novel than human expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition; 49 experts wrote, 79 reviewed, 298 reviews. Novelty mean 4.84 human, 5.64 AI, 5.81 AI plus human rerank (p<0.05). Novelty correlates r=0.725 with overall score; feasibility r<0.1 with it.
limits: Seven NLP topics. Reviewers saw idea text only.
agent_relevance: Novelty is cheap from an LLM. Feasibility is the bottleneck, so selection must weigh it.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) LLM diversity and LLM-judge tests
finding: Scaling idea generation hits duplicates. LLM judges rank ideas at near-chance level.
numbers: Only about 200 non-duplicate ideas out of 4,000 seeds per topic (similarity cutoff 0.8). Best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise) 53.3% vs inter-human consistency 56.1%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%, pairwise 45.0%; AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Top and bottom 25% of ideas only.
agent_relevance: More samples without forced difference give repeats. LLM self-scoring cannot be the selector.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: After execution, LLM ideas lose their novelty edge. Human ideas keep their scores, so rankings flip on several metrics.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each. Human ideas change by -0.010 (novelty), +0.078 (excitement), -0.052 (effectiveness). AI ideas fall by 1.049, 1.760, 1.879 on a 1-10 scale (p<0.05). Post-execution excitement 3.90 AI vs 4.48 human; effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78.
limits: 43 projects. One field (NLP).
agent_relevance: Perceived novelty is not execution value. Test a far combination before accepting it.

source: Schopf and Farber (2026) Is this idea novel? RINoBench
finding: LLMs write human-like reasons for novelty, but their scores diverge from expert gold judgments.
numbers: 1,381 research ideas with expert novelty scores on a 1-5 rubric. Macro-F1 roughly 12 to 17 across GPT-5, o3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama models. Reasoning models are not much better than non-reasoning ones.
limits: Table read from a garbled extraction; ranges only.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM novelty score is not a safe selector.

source: Schopf and Schreieder (2026) Think-Probe-Respond: improving LLMs as judges of research idea novelty
finding: LLM judges lean to 'medium novel'. Probing hidden states reduces the bias.
numbers: TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% on average over strong baselines and gives less biased judgments.
limits: Needs hidden-state access, so not usable with a closed API.
agent_relevance: Expect central-tendency bias in self-rated novelty. Use pairwise or retrieval-based checks.

source: Huang and Xie (2026) Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
finding: Equalising reference-list length reverses the small-team advantage. A one-reference-at-a-time measure recovers recognised breakthroughs better than the standard index.
numbers: About 60M publications. Six benchmarks. Their measure AUC 0.94-0.98 on all six. Standard index AUC: Turing Award 0.79, Nobel 0.73, Lasker 0.60, Test of Time 0.55, Physical Review Milestones 0.40, Science Breakthrough of the Year 0.26.
limits: Preprint (5 Oct 2026). Their own measure. Disputes b08.
agent_relevance: Even the standard index is a weak detector of famous breakthroughs. Do not tune an agent toward it.

source: Larregue and Gingras (2026) The disruption index does not measure scientific innovation
finding: At country level the index gives implausible rankings, so it is not a measure of innovation.
numbers: Share of positive-D articles: Iraq 57.5%, Nigeria 56%, others near 34.3% and 26.9%. Share is negatively correlated with number of authors.
limits: A critique of Cui et al. 2026 (Science). Single-index argument.
agent_relevance: A metric needs an external check before it drives selection.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The disruption index measures displacement between a paper and its most cited reference
finding: D is relative: how far a paper displaces its most-cited reference. This is why it differs from atypicality.
numbers: Expert survey: 20 scholars, 190 responses. Papers nominated as disruptive had mean D=0.21 (top 1%); consolidating nominations D=-0.011 (bottom 13%). AUC 0.83. Of 22M OpenAlex papers with 10 or more citations, 65% have negative dp and 32% positive. 38% of 42M papers have D>0.
limits: Survey is the 2019 survey re-analysed. Authors of the index.
agent_relevance: The decomposition matches: one-to-one replacement of the top reference versus wide recombination.

source: Yan and Ni (2026) AI-assisted writing and the reorganization of scientific knowledge
finding: After 2023, more AI-assisted writing goes with higher disruption but not with broader sourcing.
numbers: About 2M full-text articles 2021-2024. Before 2023 the link between AI-writing share and disruption is weak or negative. After 2023 it is positive in within-author, within-field models. The link to cross-field citation breadth weakens.
limits: AI-text detector is imperfect. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Disruption and atypicality can move apart.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: iterative planning and search to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM ideas
finding: Iterated retrieval of outside knowledge increases the number of unique novel LLM ideas.
numbers: Unique novel ideas rise 3.4 times from baseline over iterations; 170 seed papers; Swiss tournament scoring; judged more novel than the Si et al. baseline.
limits: Abstract and figure captions read, not the full tables. Judging partly by LLM.
agent_relevance: Retrieval from far sources works as a diversity operator.

source: Wang (2024) A content-based novelty measure for scholarly publications: a proof of concept
finding: Language-model surprise on text is used as an atypical-combination measure and checked against expert novelty ratings.
numbers: No effect size read in the abstract.
limits: Proof of concept. Small expert panel.
agent_relevance: A cheap model-based atypicality score is possible. Not tested for an agent.
